UPSTREAM'S CONTRACT: `bool rclcpp::Client<S>::service_is_ready() const`. The value IS the answer, so the near-universal idiom is `while (!client->service_is_ready()) { ... }`.

OURS (`packages/api/nros-cpp/include/rclcpp/client.hpp:222`): `Expected<bool>`, whose `explicit operator bool` is `ok_` — the PROBE-SUCCEEDED flag (`packages/api/nros-cpp/include/rclcpp/result.hpp:234`), not the readiness. A successful probe that answers "no server yet" is `Expected::ok(false)`, so `operator bool` is TRUE and `!` is false.

HOW A USER FINDS OUT: SILENTLY WRONG. The `while (!...)` loop compiles — `!` is a contextual conversion, so `explicit` does not stop it — and EXITS ON THE FIRST SUCCESSFUL "no". The ported node proceeds as if the server were up. `Expected` carries no `[[nodiscard]]` and the operand shape is legal, so nothing warns.

Disposition ADOPT: RFC-0018 forces an error channel but does not force the error channel to be the one the `bool` conversion reads. Making the conversion mean the ANSWER, or deleting the conversion so the idiom fails to compile, both satisfy the rule; silently inverting the loop does not.
